By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: ExpertLens: Activation steering features are highly interpretable
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether the features discovered by activation steering methods in large language models are interpretable, and if they align with human representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ExpertLens, a method based on activation steering, and shows that the expert neurons it identifies are stable across models and datasets, and their representations align closely with human conceptual structures.
papers.conclusion: ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for interpretability of LLMs, providing insights into model representations that align with human concepts.
papers.key_findings:
ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets.
ExpertLens representations align closely with human representations, matching inter-human alignment levels.
ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings.
ExpertLens can reconstruct human conceptual structure (domain organization).
Experts are learned from data, with larger models having more experts.
papers.limitation:
Only single-word concepts are considered.
Do not have access to training data.
Model choice (Pythia family).
Study neurons individually.
Polysemantic neurons are discussed.
future_direction: Future work will consider more complex concepts such as those expressing human values or preferences.
Exploration of alignment and its emergence in alternative model families.
Studying neurons jointly to capture additional aspects of concept representation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods in large language models (LLMs) have emerged as an effective way to perform targeted updates to enhance generated language without requiring large amounts of adaptation data. We ask whether the features discovered by activation steering methods are interpretable. We identify neurons responsible for specific concepts (e.g., ``cat'') using the ``finding experts'' method from research on activation steering and show that the ExpertLens, i.e., inspection of these neurons provides insights about model representation. We find that ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets and closely align with human representations inferred from behavioral data, matching inter-human alignment levels. ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings. By reconstructing human concept organization through ExpertLens, we show that it enables a granular view of LLM concept representation. Our findings suggest that ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for capturing and analyzing model representations.

papers.title: Representations as Language: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Interpretability
papers.research_question: What systematic structures emerge in the representations learned by transformers, and how do they relate to generalization and training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic framework for interpretability that quantifies structure in representations, identifies two phases of training, and shows how representational structure relates to generalization and model size.
papers.conclusion: The linguistically-motivated approach helps characterize training dynamics and explain generalization, and suggests that intuitions from linguistics and cognitive science about good representations transfer to deep learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct phases of training: an initial phase of in-distribution learning where representations align with token and part-of-speech information, and a second phase where representations become robust to noise and compress.
Generalization performance improves during the second phase, linking generalization to robustness to noise.
Larger models compress their representations more than smaller models.
The proposed measures (information, variation, regularity, disentanglement) can predict which models will generalize best based on their representational structure.
papers.limitation:
Some results may be particular to the hyperparameters used for training.
The entropy estimation method is an approximation and makes minimal assumptions, but is invariant to linear transformations.
future_direction: Apply the analysis to large-scale translation tasks.
Extend the approach to other levels of abstraction and other models.
papers.abstract: Large scale neural models show impressive performance across a wide array of linguistic tasks. Despite this they remain, largely, black-boxes - inducing vector-representations of their input that prove difficult to interpret. This limits our ability to understand what they learn, and when the learn it, or describe what kinds of representations generalise well out of distribution. To address this we introduce a novel approach to interpretability that looks at the mapping a model learns from sentences to representations as a kind of language in its own right. In doing so we introduce a set of information-theoretic measures that quantify how structured a model's representations are with respect to its input, and when during training that structure arises. Our measures are fast to compute, grounded in linguistic theory, and can predict which models will generalise best based on their representations. We use these measures to describe two distinct phases of training a transformer: an initial phase of in-distribution learning which reduces task loss, then a second stage where representations becoming robust to noise. Generalisation performance begins to increase during this second phase, drawing a link between generalisation and robustness to noise. Finally we look at how model size affects the structure of the representational space, showing that larger models ultimately compress their representations more than their smaller counterparts.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Understanding Gated Neurons in Transformers from Their Input-Output Functionality
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between what a neuron reads and what it writes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parameter-based method to classify gated neurons in transformers by input-output weight similarity, finding that enrichment neurons dominate early-middle layers while depletion neurons are more common in later layers.
papers.conclusion: The input-output perspective complements activation-dependent analyses and approaches that treat input and output separately, providing insights into how neurons manipulate concepts in the residual stream.
papers.key_findings:
Enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers across all 12 models studied, whereas later layers tend more towards depletion neurons.
A large proportion of neurons are input manipulators, with conditional enrichment being the most common class, especially in early-middle layers.
Many neurons exhibit double checking, where gate and input weight vectors are approximately orthogonal but intuitively represent the same concept.
The median cosine similarity between input and output weights is positive in early layers and negative in later layers, indicating a smooth transition in functionality.
Neurons rarely have prototypical weight configurations; instead, they often add novel but related information to the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method is parameter-based and therefore limited in scope; it is not designed to replace other neuron analysis methods.
Mathematical similarities of weights may not reflect semantic similarity; orthogonal vectors can represent similar concepts, and similar vectors can represent non-identical concepts.
Case studies of individual neurons may be cherry-picked, focusing on interpretable neurons in later layers, so interpretations may not generalize.
The paper provides only possible interpretations of observed phenomena, not definitive explanations.
future_direction: Extend the method to non-gated activation functions.
Study the evolution of input-output functionalities during model training.
Go beyond the analysis of single neurons to understand how neurons work together within and across classes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability researchers have attempted to understand MLP neurons of language models based on both the contexts in which they activate and their output weight vectors. They have paid little attention to a complementary aspect: the interactions between input and output. For example, when neurons detect a direction in the input, they might add much the same direction to the residual stream ("enrichment neurons") or reduce its presence ("depletion neurons"). We address this aspect by examining the cosine similarity between input and output weights of a neuron. We apply our method to 12 models and find that enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers whereas later layers tend more towards depletion. To explain this finding, we argue that enrichment neurons are largely responsible for enriching concept representations, one of the first steps of factual recall. Our input-output perspective is a complement to activation-dependent analyses and to approaches that treat input and output separately.

papers.title: Achieving stable dynamics in neural circuits
papers.research_question: How do neural circuits maintain stable dynamics in the presence of disturbance, noisy inputs and plastic change?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies contraction analysis to recurrent neural networks and identifies several mechanisms (inhibitory Hebbian plasticity, excitatory anti-Hebbian plasticity, synaptic sparsity, and excitatory-inhibitory balance) that lead to stable dynamics in biologically realistic neural circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that contraction analysis can identify mechanisms for stable dynamics in neural circuits, including inhibitory Hebbian plasticity, excitatory anti-Hebbian plasticity, synaptic sparsity, and excitatory-inhibitory balance.
papers.key_findings:
Inhibitory Hebbian plasticity and excitatory anti-Hebbian plasticity produce contraction in neural circuits.
Sparse connectivity pushes networks toward contraction.
Excitatory-inhibitory balance leads to contraction in static RNNs.
Contracting systems have fading memories, similar to Echo State Networks.
The analysis provides provable certificates of global contractive stability for nonlinear, time-varying RNNs with synaptic plasticity.
future_direction: Given an RNN, can one provide a certificate of contractive stability in a region?
papers.abstract: The brain consists of many interconnected networks with time-varying, partially autonomous activity. There are multiple sources of noise and variation yet activity has to eventually converge to a stable, reproducible state (or sequence of states) for its computations to make sense. We approached this problem from a control-theory perspective by applying contraction analysis to recurrent neural networks. This allowed us to find mechanisms for achieving stability in multiple connected networks with biologically realistic dynamics, including synaptic plasticity and time-varying inputs. These mechanisms included inhibitory Hebbian plasticity, excitatory anti-Hebbian plasticity, synaptic sparsity and excitatory-inhibitory balance. Our findings shed light on how stable computations might be achieved despite biological complexity. Crucially, our analysis is not limited to analyzing the stability of fixed geometric objects in state space (e.g points, lines, planes), but rather the stability of state trajectories which may be complex and time-varying.

papers.title: Analogical Reasoning Inside Large Language Models: Concept Vectors and the Limits of Abstraction
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor internal, invariant representations of abstract concepts like those used in analogical reasoning, and how can such representations be extracted and analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Concept Vectors (CVs), distilled from early-to-mid attention heads using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), which provide invariant linear representations for verbal concepts (e.g., antonym) and can causally guide model behavior. It finds that abstract concepts like 'previous' and 'next' lack such invariant representations, limiting generalization.
papers.conclusion: While LLMs form invariant linear representations (CVs) for verbal concepts, they lack such representations for more abstract relational concepts like 'previous' and 'next', which hinders their ability to generalize analogical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Function Vectors (FVs) are not invariant to low-level input changes (e.g., open-ended vs. multiple-choice format) and encode multiple task attributes beyond the latent concept.
Activation patching, used to identify FVs, localizes components causally important for output but fails to identify heads encoding latent conceptual information.
Concept Vectors (CVs) for verbal concepts are invariant to low-level transformations and emerge in early-to-mid layers, acting as feature detectors that can represent the correct concept even when the model's final output is incorrect.
CVs can causally guide model behavior in-context and are more portable across low-level task variations than FVs, though FVs are more effective in zero-shot settings.
Abstract concepts like 'previous' and 'next' do not form invariant linear representations in the models studied, which correlates with poor generalization on tasks requiring abstraction, such as letter-string analogies.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses exclusively on linear representations, despite evidence that LLM representations can be nonlinear, potentially missing nonlinear encodings of abstract concepts.
Conclusions are restricted to the Llama-3.1 8B and 70B models, leaving generalizability to other architectures untested.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning relies on conceptual abstractions, but it is unclear whether Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor such internal representations. We explore distilled representations from LLM activations and find that function vectors (FVs; Todd et al., 2024) - compact representations for in-context learning (ICL) tasks - are not invariant to simple input changes (e.g., open-ended vs. multiple-choice), suggesting they capture more than pure concepts. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), we localize a small set of attention heads that encode invariant concept vectors (CVs) for verbal concepts like "antonym". These CVs function as feature detectors that operate independently of the final output - meaning that a model may form a correct internal representation yet still produce an incorrect output. Furthermore, CVs can be used to causally guide model behaviour. However, for more abstract concepts like "previous" and "next", we do not observe invariant linear representations, a finding we link to generalizability issues LLMs display within these domains.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: LLM-MRI Python module: a brain scanner for LLMs
papers.research_question: How do activation patterns in transformer-based LLMs vary with different categories of text, and can neural regions be mapped to understand these patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the LLM-MRI Python module for mapping neural regions and creating graph models of activations in transformer-based LLMs to study activation patterns stimulated by different documents.
papers.conclusion: The LLM-MRI module provides a novel representation for analyzing LLM activations through neural region mapping and graph construction, facilitating intuitive understanding of how text patterns are reflected in models.
future_direction: Expand visualization options and offer quantitative metrics for graph analysis based on graph theory and complex networks.
Evaluate how significant such metrics are for understanding LLM representations of different text types.
Tune mapping and graphing functions to better capture patterns in activations.
papers.abstract: LLMs (Large Language Models) have demonstrated human-level language and knowledge acquisition skills in several tasks. However, despite the recent success and broad use, understanding how these skills are learned and encoded inside the underlying neural network is still challenging. The goal of the LLM-MRI package is to simplify the study of activation patterns in any transformer-based LLM, similarly to how MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) simplifies with biological brains. The package, written for the Python language, allows the mapping of neural regions using a parameterized reduction of the model's dimensionality. Neural regions can be visualized according to the forward-pass activations stimulated by a set of documents. Similarly, the package enables the creation of graph models representing the interlayer network of connections stimulated by a set of documents. These features allow for qualitative and quantitative assessments of the underlying structure of activations, depending on the type of documents that the LLM model is exposed to.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: Unit Testing for Concepts in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Whether neural networks are consistent with Fodor's theory of concepts, specifically whether they can be seen as implementing symbolic conceptual representations.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework of unit tests to evaluate if neural networks implement symbolic conceptual representations per Fodor's criteria, finding models succeed on groundedness, modularity, and reusability but fail on causality.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit grounded behavior and possess modular, context-independent type representations, but lack evidence of a direct causal connection between constituent and composite concepts, a key aspect of Fodor's theory.
papers.key_findings:
Models' predictions are grounded to expected perceptual features, though performance degrades with spurious correlations.
Representations of atomic concepts generalize to unseen compositions, indicating reusable type representations.
Ablating a constituent concept largely preserves other concepts, suggesting modular representations.
No direct causal link found between constituent concept representations and composite concept predictions.
Pretrained models show an inductive bias for shape over color, but pretraining does not consistently improve conceptual structure across tests.
papers.limitation:
INLP ablation only removes linear information, and diagnostic functions are restricted to linear models.
Analysis primarily treats the encode function as a block, not examining internal layers comprehensively.
future_direction: Find alternative implementations of ablate (e.g., using recent methods like Tucker et al. 2021 or Meng et al. 2022).
Expand unit tests to reflect empirical predictions from theories of concept acquisition.
Conduct a complete investigation of internal layers.
papers.abstract: Many complex problems are naturally understood in terms of symbolic concepts. For example, our concept of "cat" is related to our concepts of "ears" and "whiskers" in a non-arbitrary way. Fodor (1998) proposes one theory of concepts, which emphasizes symbolic representations related via constituency structures. Whether neural networks are consistent with such a theory is open for debate. We propose unit tests for evaluating whether a system's behavior is consistent with several key aspects of Fodor's criteria. Using a simple visual concept learning task, we evaluate several modern neural architectures against this specification. We find that models succeed on tests of groundedness, modularlity, and reusability of concepts, but that important questions about causality remain open. Resolving these will require new methods for analyzing models' internal states.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results. Our proposed approach enables the evaluation of more targeted hypotheses about the composition of meaning in the brain, expanding the range of possible scientific inferences a neuroscientist could make, and opens up new opportunities for cross-pollination between computational neuroscience and linguistics.

papers.title: The Natural Lottery Ticket Winner: Reinforcement Learning with Ordinary Neural Circuits
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether neural circuits from biological organisms (specifically C. elegans) can be considered 'natural lottery tickets' and if they can be repurposed via parameter learning to control simulated and real-world robots.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that biological neural circuits (specifically the tap-withdrawal circuit from C. elegans) can be repurposed as efficient, interpretable controllers for reinforcement learning tasks, outperforming randomly wired networks and sometimes deep learning models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that ordinary neural circuits (ONCs) are natural lottery ticket winners, providing efficient, interpretable, and high-performing controllers for reinforcement learning tasks in simulated and real-world environments.
papers.key_findings:
The Tap-Withdrawal (TW) neural circuit realizes a higher maximum flow rate compared to randomly wired networks of the same size.
Ordinary neural circuits (ONCs) trained with a random search algorithm can control various simulated and real robots, performing comparably to or better than deep learning models like MLPs and LSTMs.
ONCs are compact and sparse (77% sparser than fully-connected networks), and their internal dynamics are fully interpretable at the cell level.
ONCs can be transferred from simulation to real-world control, as demonstrated in an autonomous parking task with a rover robot.
The proposed interpretability method quantifies the contribution of individual neurons to motor decisions, revealing positive, negative, or phase-changing influences.
papers.limitation:
Scalability: the approach is limited by the current knowledge of connectomes, which is still growing.
Network design principles are ad-hoc, although statistically supported.
future_direction: Applying the approach to larger connectomes (e.g., fruit fly brain) as connectome analysis grows.
Combining graph theory with control and dynamical systems for network design.
papers.abstract: We propose a neural information processing system which is obtained by re-purposing the function of a biological neural circuit model to govern simulated and real-world control tasks. Inspired by the structure of the nervous system of the soil-worm, C. elegans, we introduce ordinary neural circuits (ONCs), defined as the model of biological neural circuits reparameterized for the control of alternative tasks. We first demonstrate that ONCs realize networks with higher maximum flow compared to arbitrary wired networks. We then learn instances of ONCs to control a series of robotic tasks, including the autonomous parking of a real-world rover robot. For reconfiguration of the purpose of the neural circuit, we adopt a search-based optimization algorithm. Ordinary neural circuits perform on par and, in some cases, significantly surpass the performance of contemporary deep learning models. ONC networks are compact, 77% sparser than their counterpart neural controllers, and their neural dynamics are fully interpretable at the cell-level.

papers.title: Systematic Generalization and Emergent Structures in Transformers Trained on Structured Tasks
papers.research_question: How and when can transformers acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization on algorithmic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Two-layer causal transformers with label-based order encoding can learn algorithmic tasks and generalize to longer sequences, exhibiting signs of task decomposition and shared computation across tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve structured algorithmic tasks and generalize systematically, with attention layers developing task decomposition and shared computation.
papers.key_findings:
Label-based order encoding enables strong length generalization in transformers on algorithmic tasks.
Two-layer transformers are sufficient to solve multi-level sorting tasks, while single-layer models fail.
Attention patterns in two-layer models show task decomposition: first layer attends to items in the same feature group, second layer attends to the next output token.
In multi-task learning, transformers can learn multiple tasks simultaneously and generalize to longer sequences, with attention heads showing shared computation across tasks.
Task-conditioned item representations are reorganized according to the task structure, showing clustering by relevant features.
papers.limitation:
Label-based encoding alone would not represent true item distance information.
The tasks are simple and synthetic, and may not capture the complexity of natural data.
future_direction: Explore learning and generalization dynamics in transformer-based agents to understand the acquisition of task-conditioned, multi-level behavioral policies in structured environments.
Characterize the degree of possible computational modularity in multi-headed attention in relation to task structures.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks have seen great success in natural language processing and machine vision, where task objectives such as next word prediction and image classification benefit from nuanced context sensitivity across high-dimensional inputs. However, there is an ongoing debate about how and when transformers can acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization. Here, we explore how well a causal transformer can perform a set of algorithmic tasks, including copying, sorting, and hierarchical compositions of these operations. We demonstrate strong generalization to sequences longer than those used in training by replacing the standard positional encoding typically used in transformers with labels arbitrarily paired with items in the sequence. We search for the layer and head configuration sufficient to solve these tasks, then probe for signs of systematic processing in latent representations and attention patterns. We show that two-layer transformers learn reliable solutions to multi-level problems, develop signs of task decomposition, and encode input items in a way that encourages the exploitation of shared computation across related tasks. These results provide key insights into how attention layers support structured computation both within a task and across multiple tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Do All Autoregressive Transformers Remember Facts the Same Way? A Cross-Architecture Analysis of Recall Mechanisms
papers.research_question: Do findings on factual recall mechanisms in GPT-style models generalize across different autoregressive Transformer architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual recall mechanisms differ across autoregressive Transformer architectures, with Qwen-based models relying more on Attention modules compared to GPT-based models which use MLP modules.
papers.conclusion: Architectural variations in autoregressive Transformers lead to different mechanisms of factual recall, emphasizing the need for architecture-aware approaches in model editing and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
In GPT-based models, MLP modules in early layers play a key role in storing factual associations.
In Qwen-based models, early Attention layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules.
Gini coefficient analysis shows that Attention modules in Qwen models have concentrated effects on factual recall.
Semantic similarity-based evaluation confirms the differential contributions of Attention and MLP modules across architectures.
The severing effects method has limitations in accurately reflecting the contribution of Attention modules to factual recall.
papers.limitation:
the internal mechanisms by which factual associations are recalled during inference remain insufficiently understood
how factual associations are dynamically accessed across different architectures remains unclear
the interpretation of such structural differences is limited
papers.abstract: Understanding how Transformer-based language models store and retrieve factual associations is critical for improving interpretability and enabling targeted model editing. Prior work, primarily on GPT-style models, has identified MLP modules in early layers as key contributors to factual recall. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize across different autoregressive architectures. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of factual recall across several models -- including GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek -- analyzing where and how factual information is encoded and accessed. Consequently, we find that Qwen-based models behave differently from previous patterns: attention modules in the earliest layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules. Our findings suggest that even within the autoregressive Transformer family, architectural variations can lead to fundamentally different mechanisms of factual recall.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Organized Attention: Softmax Invariance and Network Sparsity
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic and extrinsic structure of the self-attention mechanism in transformers, and how can it be analyzed to reveal properties like softmax invariance and network sparsity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that the self-attention mechanism is invariant to the softmax activation under appropriate regularity conditions and introduces a tensor organization method (the questionnaire algorithm) to analyze network sparsity and structure.
papers.conclusion: The intrinsic and extrinsic organization of attention heads provides theoretical insights (softmax invariance) and practical tools (sparsity analysis, visualization) for network interpretability and potential applications like model pruning.
papers.key_findings:
The self-attention mechanism can be organized to have mixed α-Holder regularity, leading to theoretical softmax invariance.
The questionnaire algorithm organizes attention heads into a hierarchical structure, enabling qualitative visualization (diffusion maps, partition trees) and quantitative analysis (expansion coefficients, l1 entropy).
The l1 entropy of expansion coefficients with respect to a bi-haar basis can identify attention heads with high and low processing activity, suggesting potential for model pruning.
The organization method reveals consistent structural patterns across different batches of data for both language and vision transformers.
The tri-haar basis expansion of the entire network tensor allows for comparative analysis of network sparsity across different models and datasets.
papers.limitation:
The softmax invariance theorem requires the attention head to be organized to have mixed α-Holder regularity, which permutes the matrix elements and loses the original intrinsic structure.
The computational implementation requires attention head dimensions to be powers of two, necessitating cropping (e.g., from 197 to 128 for ViT).
The questionnaire algorithm can be sensitive to algorithm parameters such as affinity initialization and the weight function used during the iterative EMD process.
papers.abstract: We examine the intrinsic (within the attention head) and extrinsic (amongst the attention heads) structure of the self-attention mechanism in transformers. Theoretical evidence for invariance of the self-attention mechanism to softmax activation is obtained by appealing to paradifferential calculus, (and is supported by computational examples), which relies on the intrinsic organization of the attention heads. Furthermore, we use an existing methodology for hierarchical organization of tensors to examine network structure by constructing hierarchal partition trees with respect to the query, key, and head axes of network 3-tensors. Such an organization is consequential since it allows one to profitably execute common signal processing tasks on a geometry where the organized network 3-tensors exhibit regularity. We exemplify this qualitatively, by visualizing the hierarchical organization of the tree comprised of attention heads and the diffusion map embeddings, and quantitatively by investigating network sparsity with the expansion coefficients of individual attention heads and the entire network with respect to the bi and tri-haar bases (respectively) on the space of queries, keys, and heads of the network. To showcase the utility of our theoretical and methodological findings, we provide computational examples using vision and language transformers. The ramifications of these findings are two-fold: (1) a subsequent step in interpretability analysis is theoretically admitted, and can be exploited empirically for downstream interpretability tasks (2) one can use the network 3-tensor organization for empirical network applications such as model pruning (by virtue of network sparsity) and network architecture comparison.

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for final predictions in large language models, specifically for knowledge storage?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static neuron-level attribution method based on log probability increase that outperforms other static methods, and uses it to analyze knowledge storage in attention and FFN layers of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate 'query neurons', with analysis on six knowledge types helping to understand LLM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed log probability increase method for neuron attribution achieves superior performance compared to seven other static methods across three metrics (MRR, probability, log probability).
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics (e.g., language, country, city) tends to be stored in the same heads, while knowledge with distinct semantics is stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction, despite many neurons contributing.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which in turn are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B; comparing knowledge storage across different models is essential.
Uses static methods for attribution; comparing with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods is important.
future_direction: Explore other types of knowledge beyond the six studied.
Compare knowledge storage similarities and differences across different models.
Compare static attribution methods with other methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Explaining Cognitive Phenomena with Internal Representations: A Mechanistic Perspective
papers.research_question: What criteria should an explanation of a given cognitive phenomenon meet to count as a (truly, genuinely, nontrivially, etc.) representational explanation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that representational explanations in cognitive science are a species of mechanistic explanation, and defines representational mechanisms as those that meet four conditions: structural resemblance, action-guidance, decouplability, and error-detection.
papers.conclusion: Representational mechanisms are those that use decouplable, action-guiding, error-detection-affording structural representations, and a mechanistic explanation of a cognitive phenomenon is representational if it postulates such a mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Representational explanations should be construed as a form of mechanistic explanation, answering how-questions about cognitive capacities.
A representational mechanism is one that has at least one component part whose function is to represent something, and such a component must meet four conditions: structural resemblance, action-guidance, decouplability, and error-detection.
The proposed account integrates correspondence and action-guidance approaches to representation, aiming to provide a robust notion that meets the 'job description challenge'.
Examples from cognitive science, such as emulation theory and predictive coding, can be seen as meeting the proposed conditions for representational mechanisms.
The account provides criteria for determining when a mechanistic explanation is genuinely representational, which is a step towards resolving the debate between representationalism and antirepresentationalism.
papers.limitation:
The proposed account might be too restrictive, potentially rendering many existing cognitive-scientific theories nonrepresentational.
The proposal is a general, incomplete, and highly idealized functional sketch that abstracts away from structural details.
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite the fact that the notion of internal representation has - at least according to some - a fundamental role to play in the sciences of the mind, not only has its explanatory utility been under attack for a while now, but it also remains unclear what criteria should an explanation of a given cognitive phenomenon meet to count as a (truly, genuinely, nontrivially, etc.) representational explanation in the first place. The aim of this article is to propose a solution to this latter problem. I will assume that representational explanations should be construed as a form of mechanistic explanations and proceed by proposing a general sketch of a functional architecture of a representational cognitive mechanism. According to the view on offer here, representational mechanisms are mechanisms that meet four conditions: the structural resemblance condition, the action-guidance condition, the decouplability condition, and the error-detection condition.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Emergence of Concepts in DNNs?
papers.research_question: How do existing methods identify concepts in DNNs, and how are conceptual spaces shaped by the tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression?
papers.core_contribution: Reviews and critiques methods for identifying concepts in DNNs, highlighting limitations due to reliance on partial extensions and the underexplored role of conceptual spaces shaped by accuracy-compression tradeoffs.
papers.conclusion: While DNNs can represent inferential relations between concepts, current methods for identifying these concepts are limited, and understanding holistic conceptual spaces requires new approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Network dissection, feature visualization, and TCAV methods for identifying concepts in DNNs rely on partial extensions or optimization, leading to philosophical issues like indeterminacy of reference.
DNNs can learn concepts shared by multiple predicted classes, indicating representation of non-trivial inferential relations beyond mere extensions.
Conceptual spaces in DNNs are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression, as illustrated by the Information Bottleneck framework and color naming examples.
Polysemantic neurons suggest that concepts compete for limited representational space, leading to compressed or mixed representations.
Robustness analysis by combining multiple methods could improve reliability, but absolute confirmation of concepts remains challenging.
papers.limitation:
Methods for identifying concepts rely on partial extensions, which underdetermine meaning and face indeterminacy of reference.
Existing methods are limited to extracting local or linear information, not capturing distributed or non-linear representations.
The identification of conceptual spaces and how they arise from accuracy-compression tradeoffs is underexplored.
future_direction: Combining different methods for robustness analysis to increase reliability in concept identification.
Using synthetic datasets with labeled intermediate concepts to test and improve methods for identifying concepts.
Developing methods to understand how entire conceptual spaces are formed holistically in DNNs.
papers.abstract: The present paper reviews and discusses work from computer science that proposes to identify concepts in internal representations (hidden layers) of DNNs. It is examined, first, how existing methods actually identify concepts that are supposedly represented in DNNs. Second, it is discussed how conceptual spaces -- sets of concepts in internal representations -- are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression. These issues are critically examined by drawing on philosophy. While there is evidence that DNNs able to represent non-trivial inferential relations between concepts, our ability to identify concepts is severely limited.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
