The softmax invariance theorem requires the attention head to be organized to have mixed α-Holder regularity, which permutes the matrix elements and loses the original intrinsic structure.
The computational implementation requires attention head dimensions to be powers of two, necessitating cropping (e.g., from 197 to 128 for ViT).
The questionnaire algorithm can be sensitive to algorithm parameters such as affinity initialization and the weight function used during the iterative EMD process.
papers.abstract: We examine the intrinsic (within the attention head) and extrinsic (amongst the attention heads) structure of the self-attention mechanism in transformers. Theoretical evidence for invariance of the self-attention mechanism to softmax activation is obtained by appealing to paradifferential calculus, (and is supported by computational examples), which relies on the intrinsic organization of the attention heads. Furthermore, we use an existing methodology for hierarchical organization of tensors to examine network structure by constructing hierarchal partition trees with respect to the query, key, and head axes of network 3-tensors. Such an organization is consequential since it allows one to profitably execute common signal processing tasks on a geometry where the organized network 3-tensors exhibit regularity. We exemplify this qualitatively, by visualizing the hierarchical organization of the tree comprised of attention heads and the diffusion map embeddings, and quantitatively by investigating network sparsity with the expansion coefficients of individual attention heads and the entire network with respect to the bi and tri-haar bases (respectively) on the space of queries, keys, and heads of the network. To showcase the utility of our theoretical and methodological findings, we provide computational examples using vision and language transformers. The ramifications of these findings are two-fold: (1) a subsequent step in interpretability analysis is theoretically admitted, and can be exploited empirically for downstream interpretability tasks (2) one can use the network 3-tensor organization for empirical network applications such as model pruning (by virtue of network sparsity) and network architecture comparison.

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for final predictions in large language models, specifically for knowledge storage?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static neuron-level attribution method based on log probability increase that outperforms other static methods, and uses it to analyze knowledge storage in attention and FFN layers of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate 'query neurons', with analysis on six knowledge types helping to understand LLM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed log probability increase method for neuron attribution achieves superior performance compared to seven other static methods across three metrics (MRR, probability, log probability).
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics (e.g., language, country, city) tends to be stored in the same heads, while knowledge with distinct semantics is stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction, despite many neurons contributing.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which in turn are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B; comparing knowledge storage across different models is essential.
Uses static methods for attribution; comparing with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods is important.
future_direction: Explore other types of knowledge beyond the six studied.
Compare knowledge storage similarities and differences across different models.
Compare static attribution methods with other methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand the mechanism of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify task-detection and task-execution features in the in-context learning circuit of large language models, and introduces the Task Vector Cleaning algorithm to decompose task vectors into interpretable features.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance understanding of in-context learning mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders as a powerful tool for interpretability research on larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be used to analyze in-context learning in larger models like Gemma-1 2B, scaling up circuit analysis.
Task-execution features encode task knowledge and can causally induce task zero-shot performance.
Task-detection features identify tasks from the prompt and are causally linked to execution features via attention and MLP sublayers.
The Task Vector Cleaning algorithm effectively decomposes task vectors into sparse, interpretable features while preserving their effect on loss.
The in-context learning circuit involves interaction between detection and execution features through attention and MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Circuit search was constrained to intermediate layers due to early layers processing token-level information and having lower quality Indirect Effect approximations.
Hundreds of features needed to be ablated to achieve significant faithfulness degradation, unlike prior work which required fewer.
Negative steering experiments showed lower task specificity, indicating steering experiments alone may not suffice for comprehensive analysis.
future_direction: Improving SAE training to yield more monosemantic features.
Scaling circuit analysis to even larger models.
Applying these techniques to more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. This aligns with prior work showing that ICL is mediated by task vectors. We further demonstrate that these task vectors are well approximated by a sparse sum of SAE latents, including these task-execution features. To explore the ICL mechanism, we adapt the sparse feature circuits methodology of Marks et al. (2024) to work for the much larger Gemma-1 2B model, with 30 times as many parameters, and to the more complex task of ICL. Through circuit finding, we discover task-detecting features with corresponding SAE latents that activate earlier in the prompt, that detect when tasks have been performed. They are causally linked with task-execution features through the attention and MLP sublayers.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Explaining Cognitive Phenomena with Internal Representations: A Mechanistic Perspective
papers.research_question: What criteria should an explanation of a given cognitive phenomenon meet to count as a (truly, genuinely, nontrivially, etc.) representational explanation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that representational explanations in cognitive science are a species of mechanistic explanation, and defines representational mechanisms as those that meet four conditions: structural resemblance, action-guidance, decouplability, and error-detection.
papers.conclusion: Representational mechanisms are those that use decouplable, action-guiding, error-detection-affording structural representations, and a mechanistic explanation of a cognitive phenomenon is representational if it postulates such a mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Representational explanations should be construed as a form of mechanistic explanation, answering how-questions about cognitive capacities.
A representational mechanism is one that has at least one component part whose function is to represent something, and such a component must meet four conditions: structural resemblance, action-guidance, decouplability, and error-detection.
The proposed account integrates correspondence and action-guidance approaches to representation, aiming to provide a robust notion that meets the 'job description challenge'.
Examples from cognitive science, such as emulation theory and predictive coding, can be seen as meeting the proposed conditions for representational mechanisms.
The account provides criteria for determining when a mechanistic explanation is genuinely representational, which is a step towards resolving the debate between representationalism and antirepresentationalism.
papers.limitation:
The proposed account might be too restrictive, potentially rendering many existing cognitive-scientific theories nonrepresentational.
The proposal is a general, incomplete, and highly idealized functional sketch that abstracts away from structural details.
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite the fact that the notion of internal representation has - at least according to some - a fundamental role to play in the sciences of the mind, not only has its explanatory utility been under attack for a while now, but it also remains unclear what criteria should an explanation of a given cognitive phenomenon meet to count as a (truly, genuinely, nontrivially, etc.) representational explanation in the first place. The aim of this article is to propose a solution to this latter problem. I will assume that representational explanations should be construed as a form of mechanistic explanations and proceed by proposing a general sketch of a functional architecture of a representational cognitive mechanism. According to the view on offer here, representational mechanisms are mechanisms that meet four conditions: the structural resemblance condition, the action-guidance condition, the decouplability condition, and the error-detection condition.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Emergence of Concepts in DNNs?
papers.research_question: How do existing methods identify concepts in DNNs, and how are conceptual spaces shaped by the tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression?
papers.core_contribution: Reviews and critiques methods for identifying concepts in DNNs, highlighting limitations due to reliance on partial extensions and the underexplored role of conceptual spaces shaped by accuracy-compression tradeoffs.
papers.conclusion: While DNNs can represent inferential relations between concepts, current methods for identifying these concepts are limited, and understanding holistic conceptual spaces requires new approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Network dissection, feature visualization, and TCAV methods for identifying concepts in DNNs rely on partial extensions or optimization, leading to philosophical issues like indeterminacy of reference.
DNNs can learn concepts shared by multiple predicted classes, indicating representation of non-trivial inferential relations beyond mere extensions.
Conceptual spaces in DNNs are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression, as illustrated by the Information Bottleneck framework and color naming examples.
Polysemantic neurons suggest that concepts compete for limited representational space, leading to compressed or mixed representations.
Robustness analysis by combining multiple methods could improve reliability, but absolute confirmation of concepts remains challenging.
papers.limitation:
Methods for identifying concepts rely on partial extensions, which underdetermine meaning and face indeterminacy of reference.
Existing methods are limited to extracting local or linear information, not capturing distributed or non-linear representations.
The identification of conceptual spaces and how they arise from accuracy-compression tradeoffs is underexplored.
future_direction: Combining different methods for robustness analysis to increase reliability in concept identification.
Using synthetic datasets with labeled intermediate concepts to test and improve methods for identifying concepts.
Developing methods to understand how entire conceptual spaces are formed holistically in DNNs.
papers.abstract: The present paper reviews and discusses work from computer science that proposes to identify concepts in internal representations (hidden layers) of DNNs. It is examined, first, how existing methods actually identify concepts that are supposedly represented in DNNs. Second, it is discussed how conceptual spaces -- sets of concepts in internal representations -- are shaped by a tradeoff between predictive accuracy and compression. These issues are critically examined by drawing on philosophy. While there is evidence that DNNs able to represent non-trivial inferential relations between concepts, our ability to identify concepts is severely limited.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Response Uncertainty and Probe Modeling: Two Sides of the Same Coin in LLM Interpretability?
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance? Specifically, does a correlation exist, and what mechanisms underlie it?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates a strong negative correlation between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance, and provides a feature-attribution-based explanation showing that higher uncertainty corresponds to more dispersed important features, making probing harder.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance, with higher uncertainty linked to more dispersed important features, making probing harder. It also shows examples where low uncertainty corresponds to interpretable embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong negative correlation between response uncertainty and probe performance across multiple datasets and LLMs.
High response uncertainty is associated with a larger set of important features in the LLM's representations, which hinders probe performance.
The probe model and LLM generation rely on similar sets of features, as shown by feature removal experiments.
The correlation is robust to variations in generation temperature, sliding window parameters, and prompt templates.
Using response uncertainty, examples where LLM embeddings align with human knowledge (e.g., brand categories, time cycles) can be identified.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between probe weights and prompt embeddings is not well understood.
The correlation is only observed in instruction-tuned models, not base LLMs.
The encoding and decoding processes for concepts are not fully understood.
A unified interpretability framework is needed.
future_direction: Investigating the analogy between prompts and probes.
Studying parameter changes during instruction tuning.
Developing a unified interpretability framework.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques have shown promise in revealing how LLMs encode human-interpretable concepts, particularly when applied to curated datasets. However, the factors governing a dataset's suitability for effective probe training are not well-understood. This study hypothesizes that probe performance on such datasets reflects characteristics of both the LLM's generated responses and its internal feature space. Through quantitative analysis of probe performance and LLM response uncertainty across a series of tasks, we find a strong correlation: improved probe performance consistently corresponds to a reduction in response uncertainty, and vice versa. Subsequently, we delve deeper into this correlation through the lens of feature importance analysis. Our findings indicate that high LLM response variance is associated with a larger set of important features, which poses a greater challenge for probe models and often results in diminished performance. Moreover, leveraging the insights from response uncertainty analysis, we are able to identify concrete examples where LLM representations align with human knowledge across diverse domains, offering additional evidence of interpretable reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Large Language Model Alignment: Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.research_question: This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examines how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies, and identifies key challenges and future research directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLM alignment, analyzing progress, challenges, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability is essential for understanding and aligning LLMs, but fundamental challenges remain. Future work must focus on scalable automated methods, rigorous validation, and pluralistic alignment that respects diverse human values.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability has enabled targeted interventions for alignment, such as steering model behavior and identifying harmful circuits.
Fundamental challenges include superposition, polysemanticity, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models.
Interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies like RLHF, constitutional AI, and scalable oversight.
Future research should focus on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization, and interpretability-driven alignment techniques.
The field must address pluralistic alignment to respect diverse human values and cultures.
papers.limitation:
False confidence: Interpretability might provide misleading confidence in model safety if interpretations are incorrect or incomplete.
Arms race dynamics: Interpretability tools could be used to make models better at deception or to remove safety mechanisms.
Diminishing returns: The cost of interpretability may grow faster than model capabilities, potentially making comprehensive understanding of future systems intractable.
Philosophical challenges: Even perfect interpretability may not resolve fundamental questions about consciousness, moral status, or value alignment in AI systems.
future_direction: Automated interpretability at scale, including scalable circuit discovery and automated description generation.
Cross-model generalization, investigating universal circuits and transfer of interventions.
Interpretability-first alignment, including mechanistic anomaly detection and transparent architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their internal decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Mechanistic interpretability (i.e., the systematic study of how neural networks implement algorithms through their learned representations and computational structures) has emerged as a critical research direction for understanding and aligning these models. This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examining methods ranging from circuit discovery to feature visualization, activation steering, and causal intervention. We analyze how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies including reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), constitutional AI, and scalable oversight. Key challenges are identified, including the superposition hypothesis, polysemanticity of neurons, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models. We propose future research directions focusing on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization of circuits, and the development of interpretability-driven alignment techniques that can scale to frontier models.

papers.title: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: How do minimal circuits for indirect object identification emerge in attention-only transformers trained from scratch on a symbolic task?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that task-constrained training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits for indirect object identification in attention-only transformers.
papers.conclusion: Task-constrained training can produce parsimonious and interpretable circuits, offering insight into computational motifs underlying reasoning in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer, two-head attention-only transformer achieves perfect accuracy on the symbolic IOI task.
The two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution.
A two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance through composition across layers via query-value interactions.
Positional embeddings improve accuracy and interpretability but are not strictly necessary for the task.
The circuits in task-constrained models are more parsimonious than those in broadly pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer large language models (LLMs) into human-understandable computational circuits. However, the complexity of pretrained models often obscures the minimal mechanisms required for specific reasoning tasks. In this work, we train small, attention-only transformers from scratch on a symbolic version of the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task -- a benchmark for studying coreference -- like reasoning in transformers. Surprisingly, a single-layer model with only two attention heads achieves perfect IOI accuracy, despite lacking MLPs and normalization layers. Through residual stream decomposition, spectral analysis, and embedding interventions, we find that the two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution. Furthermore, we show that a two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance by composing information across layers through query-value interactions. These results demonstrate that task-specific training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits, offering a controlled testbed for probing the computational foundations of transformer reasoning.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Neural Attention: A Novel Mechanism for Enhanced Expressive Power in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Can replacing the dot product in transformer attention with a feed-forward network enhance the model's expressive power and predictive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neural Attention, a method that replaces the dot product in transformer attention with a feed-forward network to capture nonlinear relationships, demonstrating improved performance on language modeling and image classification tasks.
papers.conclusion: Neural Attention enhances the predictive capabilities of transformers by capturing nonlinear dependencies, and its practical overhead can be managed, making it a promising direction for improving transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
Neural Attention reduces perplexity on WikiText-103 by up to 2.19% compared to standard Dot-Product Attention.
Neural Attention improves validation accuracy on CIFAR-10 by 3.0 percentage points and on CIFAR-100 by 4.26 percentage points.
The computational overhead of Neural Attention can be mitigated by applying it only in the first transformer layer and using linear down-projection of the embedding dimension.
Neural Attention with a down-projection dimension as low as 2 still outperforms Dot-Product Attention, suggesting it is a low-rank operation.
The method is modular and can be integrated into existing transformer architectures with minimal changes.
papers.limitation: Neural Attention introduces higher computational and memory requirements compared to standard Dot-Product Attention.
future_direction: Applying Neural Attention during the pretraining phase of large-scale conversational AI models.
Exploring applications in edge computing where increased performance with minimal efficiency loss is valuable.
Investigating hybrid attention architectures that selectively apply Neural Attention in critical layers to balance efficiency and representational power.
papers.abstract: Transformer models typically calculate attention matrices using dot products, which have limitations when capturing nonlinear relationships between embedding vectors. We propose Neural Attention, a technique that replaces dot products with feed-forward networks, enabling a more expressive representation of relationships between tokens. This approach modifies only the attention matrix calculation while preserving the matrix dimensions, making it easily adaptable to existing transformer-based architectures. We provide a detailed mathematical justification for why Neural Attention increases representational capacity and conduct controlled experiments to validate this claim. When comparing Neural Attention and Dot-Product Attention, NLP experiments on WikiText-103 show a reduction in perplexity of over 2 percent. Similarly, experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show improvements in accuracy of more than 4 percentage points for image classification tasks. While Neural Attention introduces higher computational demands, we develop techniques to mitigate these challenges, ensuring practical usability without sacrificing the increased expressivity it provides. This work establishes Neural Attention as an effective means of enhancing the predictive capabilities of transformer models across a variety of applications. The code for all experiments is available at https://github.com/awayfromzel/neural-attention-research.

papers.title: Placing language in an integrated understanding system: Next steps toward human-level performance in neural language models
papers.research_question: What is the role of language in human intelligence and how can we extend current machine language models to achieve human-level language understanding by integrating language with other modalities and memory systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for building an integrated understanding system that combines insights from cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using query-based attention and memory systems to extend current language models toward human-level language understanding.
papers.conclusion: Combining insights from neuroscience and AI will take us closer to human-level language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Current language models are limited by their focus on language-internal tasks and lack of memory for remote information.
The human brain integrates language with other modalities and uses complementary learning systems (neocortex and medial temporal lobe) for understanding.
Query-based attention is a key innovation that can be extended to integrate multiple modalities and memory.
Future models should incorporate an MTL-like memory to handle remote information and improve data efficiency.
Understanding should be seen as constructing situation representations, which are compositional and grounded in multi-sensory experience.
papers.limitation: The proposed sketch leaves important issues open and will require substantial development.
future_direction: Incorporating an MTL-like memory to allow the use of remote information beyond the current episode.
Integrating a frontal lobe-like subsystem to guide processing according to task demands.
Extending the approach beyond concrete situations to abstract ones involving laws, belief systems, and scientific theories.
papers.abstract: Language is crucial for human intelligence, but what exactly is its role? We take language to be a part of a system for understanding and communicating about situations. In humans, these abilities emerge gradually from experience and depend on domain-general principles of biological neural networks: connection-based learning, distributed representation, and context-sensitive, mutual constraint satisfaction-based processing. Current artificial language processing systems rely on the same domain general principles, embodied in artificial neural networks. Indeed, recent progress in this field depends on query-based attention, which extends the ability of these systems to exploit context and has contributed to remarkable breakthroughs. Nevertheless, most current models focus exclusively on language-internal tasks, limiting their ability to perform tasks that depend on understanding situations. These systems also lack memory for the contents of prior situations outside of a fixed contextual span. We describe the organization of the brain's distributed understanding system, which includes a fast learning system that addresses the memory problem. We sketch a framework for future models of understanding drawing equally on cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence and exploiting query-based attention. We highlight relevant current directions and consider further developments needed to fully capture human-level language understanding in a computational system.

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we detect and resolve knowledge conflicts in LLMs by steering their internal activations at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in LLM activations, effectively steering knowledge selection behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SPARE offers an effective and efficient way to control knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected in the residual stream of LLMs, especially in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively controls knowledge selection, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
SPARE requires only a small set of SAE features (e.g., <0.05% for Gemma2-9B) for effective control.
The residual stream shows skewed representations when models use contextual knowledge compared to parametric knowledge.
Middle layers are more steerable for knowledge selection behavior.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pre-trained SAEs, which may not be available for all models.
Generalization to other types of tasks or conflicts (e.g., complex reasoning, multi-hop questions) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in binary terms (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), while real-world decisions may require more nuance.
papers.abstract: Yu Zhao, Alessio Devoto, Giwon Hong, Xiaotang Du, Aryo Pradipta Gema, Hongru Wang, Xuanli He, Kam-Fai Wong, Pasquale Minervini. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Visualizing and Benchmarking LLM Factual Hallucination Tendencies via Internal State Analysis and Clustering
papers.research_question: How do false or fabricated citations affect LLM hallucination tendencies, and how do hallucinations manifest in the internal states of models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the FalseCite dataset for benchmarking LLM hallucination with deceptive citations and shows false citations increase hallucination rates, especially in smaller models. Also visualizes and clusters internal state vectors to analyze hallucination signals.
papers.conclusion: The FalseCite benchmark provides a foundation for evaluating and mitigating hallucinations in future LLM research, and internal state analysis offers a way to visualize hallucination signals.
papers.key_findings:
False citations consistently amplify hallucination behavior across all tested models.
Randomly paired citations produce the strongest increase in hallucination rates, while semantically aligned citations produce a smaller but still noticeable increase.
GPT-4o-mini had the smallest baseline hallucination rate but the largest absolute increase when presented with false citations.
Hidden state vectors, when visualized, trace out a distinct horn-like shape across layers.
Clustering of hidden state vectors reveals some clusters with slightly higher hallucination rates.
papers.limitation: Reliance on GPT-4.1 as an expert model for labeling hallucinations due to lack of time and access to RAG models; the expert model also cannot verify citation authenticity as it lacks internet access.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often hallucinate, generating nonsensical or false information that can be especially harmful in sensitive fields such as medicine or law. To study this phenomenon systematically, we introduce FalseCite, a curated dataset designed to capture and benchmark hallucinated responses induced by misleading or fabricated citations. Running GPT-4o-mini, Falcon-7B, and Mistral 7-B through FalseCite, we observed a noticeable increase in hallucination activity for false claims with deceptive citations, especially in GPT-4o-mini. Using the responses from FalseCite, we can also analyze the internal states of hallucinating models, visualizing and clustering the hidden state vectors. From this analysis, we noticed that the hidden state vectors, regardless of hallucination or non-hallucination, tend to trace out a distinct horn-like shape. Our work underscores FalseCite's potential as a foundation for evaluating and mitigating hallucinations in future LLM research.

papers.title: Aligning Artificial Neural Networks and Ontologies towards Explainable AI
papers.research_question: Whether it is possible to relate the activations of a neural network with human-defined concepts from an ontology to generate symbolic justifications for the output of that neural network.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to generate human-comprehensible justifications for a neural network's output by mapping its internal activations to concepts from an ontology using small classifiers called mapping networks.
papers.conclusion: It is possible to leverage the knowledge hidden in a neural network's architecture to map its activations to ontological concepts and generate symbolic, human-comprehensible justifications for its output, increasing interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Mapping networks can extract human-defined ontological concepts from a neural network's activations if the concepts are relevant to the network's task.
Mapping networks require less training data and achieve higher accuracy than training a separate convolutional neural network to predict the same concepts from raw images.
An occlusion procedure shows that mapping networks correctly localize the visual features corresponding to the concepts they are trained to identify.
A feature selection procedure (Input Reduce) can significantly reduce the number of input features (activations) required for mapping networks while maintaining accuracy.
Using the extracted concepts and the ontology, symbolic justifications for the neural network's output can be generated, with correct justifications found in most test cases.
papers.limitation: The justifications obtained are not necessarily a representation of how neural networks really reach their outputs, but rather plausible and understandable justifications for how they might have achieved their results.
future_direction: Explore in-depth the extraction of justifications based on the ontology and the results of the mapping networks.
Investigate the usage of this method to search for learned biases in trained neural networks.
Use the method as a way to search for errors, missing axioms, or missing relations in ontologies.
papers.abstract: Neural networks have been the key to solve a variety of different problems. However, neural network models are still regarded as black boxes, since they do not provide any human-interpretable evidence as to why they output a certain result. We address this issue by leveraging on ontologies and building small classifiers that map a neural network model's internal state to concepts from an ontology, enabling the generation of symbolic justifications for the output of neural network models. Using an image classification problem as testing ground, we discuss how to map the internal state of a neural network to the concepts of an ontology, examine whether the results obtained by the established mappings match our understanding of the mapped concepts, and analyze the justifications obtained through this method.

papers.title: Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve factual knowledge? The paper investigates the mechanistic story behind factual recall, focusing on prompts of the form 'Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of ____.'
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall in LLMs is achieved through an additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs), termed the 'additive motif', and extends direct logit attribution to attribute attention head outputs to individual source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall in LLMs is achieved through additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms, and this additive motif may be a general principle in how models compute.
papers.key_findings:
There are four distinct mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs) that additively combine to produce factual recall.
Each mechanism independently contributes to the correct logit, and their sum results in constructive interference, even if individual mechanisms are insufficient alone.
The additive motif explains why models often produce incorrect attributes alongside correct ones.
Extending direct logit attribution to attribute head outputs to source tokens reveals mixed heads as two separate additive updates from subject and relation tokens.
The work highlights a limitation of narrow circuit analysis that ignores multiple sources of information in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small and hand-written, which may limit generalizability.
The analysis is limited to a specific prompting format and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Understanding correlation and superposition in feature representations
Understanding MLP neurons in detail
Studying how different prompting setups affect factual recall mechanisms
papers.abstract: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form `Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. We term this generic phenomena the additive motif: models compute through summing up multiple independent contributions. Each mechanism's contribution may be insufficient alone, but summing results in constructive interfere on the correct answer. In addition, we extend the method of direct logit attribution to attribute an attention head's output to individual source tokens. We use this technique to unpack what we call `mixed heads' -- which are themselves a pair of two separate additive updates from different source tokens.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: From Concepts to Components: Concept-Agnostic Attention Module Discovery in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we map arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads in transformer models in a concept-agnostic way, and how can we intervene on these modules to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a concept-agnostic method (SAMD) to map arbitrary concepts to sparse sets of attention heads in transformers, and a simple intervention strategy (SAMI) to diminish or amplify these concepts by scaling the heads' outputs with a single scalar parameter.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables concept-agnostic attention head attribution and effective intervention for arbitrary concepts in transformers, offering new insights into the role of attention in concept encoding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge for a wide variety of concepts is sparsely encoded in only 3-10 attention heads across transformer models.
The locations of concept-associated attention modules remain stable before and after LLM post-training, supporting the superficial alignment hypothesis.
The 'French' module is located in later layers, confirming prior work that multilingual LLMs 'think' in English and translate later.
Diminishing the safety module via SAMI increases jailbreaking success on HarmBench by up to +72.7%.
Amplifying the reasoning module improves performance on GSM8K by +1.6%, and suppressing a recognition module in a ViT reduces target label accuracy to 0%.
papers.limitation:
The method does not establish causality for the identified modules, which could be overcomplete or incomplete.
No theoretical sample complexity or stability analysis is provided.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance across language and vision tasks. This success drives the imperative to interpret their internal mechanisms with the dual goals of enhancing performance and improving behavioral control. Attribution methods help advance interpretability by assigning model outputs associated with a target concept to specific model components. Current attribution research primarily studies multi-layer perceptron neurons and addresses relatively simple concepts such as factual associations (e.g., Paris is located in France). This focus tends to overlook the impact of the attention mechanism and lacks a unified approach for analyzing more complex concepts. To fill these gaps, we introduce Scalable Attention Module Discovery (SAMD), a concept-agnostic method for mapping arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads of general transformer models. We accomplish this by representing each concept as a vector, calculating its cosine similarity with each attention head, and selecting the TopK-scoring heads to construct the concept-associated attention module. We then propose Scalar Attention Module Intervention (SAMI), a simple strategy to diminish or amplify the effects of a concept by adjusting the attention module using only a single scalar parameter. Empirically, we demonstrate SAMD on concepts of varying complexity, and visualize the locations of their corresponding modules. Our results demonstrate that module locations remain stable before and after LLM post-training, and confirm prior work on the mechanics of LLM multilingualism. Through SAMI, we facilitate jailbreaking on HarmBench (+72.7%) by diminishing "safety" and improve performance on the GSM8K benchmark (+1.6%) by amplifying "reasoning". Lastly, we highlight the domain-agnostic nature of our approach by suppressing the image classification accuracy of vision transformers on ImageNet.

papers.title: Lessons from Neuroscience for AI: How integrating Actions, Compositional Structure and Episodic Memory could enable Safe, Interpretable and Human-Like AI
papers.research_question: How can integrating actions, compositional structure, and episodic memory from predictive coding models of the brain address deficiencies in current foundation models such as hallucinations, lack of grounding, and energy inefficiency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that integrating actions, compositional structure, and episodic memory from neuroscience into foundation models can address deficiencies such as hallucinations, lack of grounding, and energy inefficiency, leading to safer, more interpretable, and human-like AI.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rekindling the exchange between brain science and AI will pave the way towards safe and interpretable human-centered AI.
papers.key_findings:
Current foundation models lack integration of actions, which is crucial for grounding and world modeling.
Hierarchical compositional structure is missing, limiting reuse and efficient processing.
Episodic memory is not properly incorporated, affecting context retention and consolidation.
Integrating these components can reduce hallucinations and improve safety and interpretability.
A brain-inspired architecture combining world models, policy networks, and memory can enhance foundation models.
papers.abstract: The phenomenal advances in large language models (LLMs) and other foundation models over the past few years have been based on optimizing large-scale transformer models on the surprisingly simple objective of minimizing next-token prediction loss, a form of predictive coding that is also the backbone of an increasingly popular model of brain function in neuroscience and cognitive science. However, current foundation models ignore three other important components of state-of-the-art predictive coding models: tight integration of actions with generative models, hierarchical compositional structure, and episodic memory. We propose that to achieve safe, interpretable, energy-efficient, and human-like AI, foundation models should integrate actions, at multiple scales of abstraction, with a compositional generative architecture and episodic memory. We present recent evidence from neuroscience and cognitive science on the importance of each of these components. We describe how the addition of these missing components to foundation models could help address some of their current deficiencies: hallucinations and superficial understanding of concepts due to lack of grounding, a missing sense of agency/responsibility due to lack of control, threats to safety and trustworthiness due to lack of interpretability, and energy inefficiency.
